newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FOCUS - Red-hot Taipei stocks defy Taiwan-China worry.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Red-hot Taipei stocks defy Taiwan-China worry.

text.p: What a difference a year and a couple months can make, especially if your bitter adversary keeps its three million troops in their barracks.

In mid-March 1996, Taiwan's stock investors were all but running for the foxholes as unarmed ballistic missiles fired from communist China were splashing down into target zones just outside Taiwan's main ports.

Rattled by eight months of Beijing's military menacing, investors sank their funds into gold and greenbacks -- and sank the shell-shocked Taiwan share index to an intraday low 4,672.67 on March 12 on turnover of T$22 billion.

On Wednesday, Taiwan's sizzling stock index spiked briefly to 9,415.58 to notch a dramatic psychological milestone -- a rise of more than 100 percent in the 16 relatively peaceful months since the Taiwan straits missile crisis.
"It's an incredible achievement," said Nomura Securities analyst Amy Huang.
"This shows that Taiwan's economic fundamentals, which were shaken by the war games, have recovered gradually ever since."

By Wednesday's close, profit-taking above 9,400 had eroded the day's gains and the index finished up 57.41 points or 0.62 percent at 9,362.68 -- still a seven-year closing high but just 99.53 percent above the political nadir of March 12, 1996.
Significantly, turnover was a screaming T$212.9 billion (US$7.6 billion) -- fully 860 percent more than March 12, 1996, yet well off the all-time high T$251 billion of June 19.
"We are loaded, such a cash-rich society, and people are using their money," said BZW Securities sales chief Alex Lee.
"Even though economic recovery is not in place yet, this really shows the confidence from the political side."

Noting that corporate earnings are on track to grow about 17 percent in 1997, Lee cautioned that Taiwan stocks were "a little over-valued" and that a stronger recovery was needed to revive other key sectors -- chiefly the long-slumping property market.
"If we find any signals of fundamental recovery on the economic front, that probably would drive liquidity to other places," he said.

Analysts say the stock rally remains broad and has shown few signs of the kind of "bubble" build-up that preceded Taiwan's crash of 1990, when the index fell 80 percent from a peak of 12,495 in just eight months.

One concern is that some 60 percent of recent share turnover has focused on one sector, electronics, where price/earning ratios have risen to average nearly 30, a level that would have been unacceptably high a year ago.

With torrents of liquidity flowing into stocks from the money and foreign exchange markets, analysts warn of a growing temptation for the central bank to tighten liquidity -- though in doing so it could risk chilling Taiwan's fragile recovery.
Taiwan's economic growth has slowed in each of the past two years, registering a disappointing 5.71 percent in 1996, but is on track to come in well above six percent in 1997.
Recovery in the property sector is seen as crucial.

As ever, Taiwan's economic outlook rises or falls on the political winds blowing from Beijing, and increasingly on the health of China's burgeoning "socialist market economy", where Taiwan interests have tied up US$30 billion in investment.

Although Taipei and Beijing have not been on speaking terms since mid-1995 and deep tensions colour their huge "unofficial" trade and investment ties, China has softened its tone toward Taiwan, which it sees as a renegade province.

China's army, which menaced Taiwan with months of live-fire war games before its historic March 1996 presidential polls, largely has returned to its barracks, though it still pledges to retake the island by force if Taipei opts for independence.

Beijing has used its resumption of sovereignty over Hong Kong to woo Taiwan, saying the success of what it promises will be hands-off management of the territory will persuade Taiwan to accept reunion under similar terms of high local autonomy.
